title: Saying no politely
teaches: Rate limits and load shedding: token buckets, sliding windows, shared counters, and where the limiter sits

blocks.text: In February 2017 Paul Tarjan, an engineer at Stripe, published a post on how the company keeps its payments API standing. Stripe's API is one set of servers shared by every business that takes card payments through it, from a bakery's web shop to an airline. Each business is a **tenant**, one customer of a shared service. Most tenants send a steady trickle of requests. Now and then one of them sends a flood, such as a script stuck in a loop that retries a failed call with no pause, a nightly report that pages through every charge since the account was opened, or a load test pointed at production by mistake. Every request in that flood consumes a thread, a database connection and several milliseconds of CPU time that the other tenants need. Without a rate limiter, one customer's bug causes an outage for everyone, which is the cascading failure we saw spread through Netflix's services in lesson 18, *Breaking things on purpose*.

Stripe's solution was a set of four limiters, and Tarjan explained what each one does and why it is there. In this lesson, you will design a rate limiter yourself first, then compare it with what Stripe built. Using our own round numbers, we will target an API with **a million API keys**, **50,000 requests a second** at the daily peak, a default limit of **100 requests a second per key**, and a latency budget of well under 1 ms per request for the limiter itself. Before drawing any architecture diagrams, we must define the requirements.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: If you build a limiter to stop every kind of abuse, it will handle none of them well. Some tasks that sound like rate limiting belong to other parts of the system: the network edge drops a flood of junk packets before it reaches the application (lesson 19), and the security team handles stolen API keys rather than the counting logic. Sort the tasks below to see why each belongs where it does.

blocks.caption: Possible jobs for the limiter. Some belong in the design; some belong to another part of the system.

options.ask: In this design, or somewhere else?

items.name: Per-key rate caps
items.clue: Cap each API key at a sustained rate, with short bursts allowed
items.why: The core requirement: one key's traffic must not crowd out the rest.

items.name: When to retry
items.clue: Tell a refused client when to try again
items.why: A 429 with Retry-After turns blind retries into a wait the client can plan around.

items.name: Payments in an overload
items.clue: Keep payments flowing when the whole fleet is short of capacity
items.why: Per-key limits can't help when every key is within its limit and the total is still too much; that needs shedding by priority.

items.name: Limits as data
items.clue: Change a customer's limit without a deploy
items.why: Limits are data. Support staff raise them for big customers, so they live in a table, not in code.

items.name: Packet floods
items.clue: Drop a flood of 100 Gb/s of junk packets
items.why: That has to be stopped at the network's edge, long before an HTTP request is parsed and an API key read.

items.name: Billing overage
items.clue: Bill customers for requests over their plan
items.why: Billing needs exact counts kept for months; the limiter's counts can be approximate and forgotten within minutes.

items.name: Stolen keys
items.clue: Notice that a key has been stolen
items.why: That is fraud detection, which looks at where and how a key is used, not at how fast.

items.name: Exact counts
items.clue: Count every request exactly, never one over
items.why: Exactness would cost a coordinated write per request. Letting a client run 5% over its limit for a second hurts nobody.

blocks.text: We can write the requirements down briefly. **Functional:** count each key's requests against its limit and refuse the excess; tell refused clients when to retry; under fleet-wide overload, drop the least important work first; and read limits from a configuration table. **Non-functional:** add under 1 ms of latency at the 99th percentile; degrade gracefully when a limiter machine dies; and stay accurate to within about 10%, because a rate limit is a guard rail rather than an invoice. That tolerance for error matters later. Because a count may be slightly inaccurate, gateways can fetch tokens in batches and regions can each hold part of a limit, as we will see below, instead of querying one central counter on every request.

The simplest limiter uses a **fixed window**, keeping one counter per key per minute and resetting it when the minute turns. This requires one integer per key and one increment per request. Its flaw appears at the boundary between two windows. Before you choose a counting algorithm, estimate how much extra traffic that boundary flaw lets through.

blocks.caption: Three minutes of one client's requests against a limit of 100 requests a minute: a slow trickle, and two bursts of 90 requests that straddle the end of the first minute. Dashed lines mark where fixed windows start.
blocks.task: Guess, then try another way of counting

blocks.text: The two bursts land in different windows, so each window counts fewer than 100 requests and lets almost all of them through. With a background trickle of one request every 3 seconds, the limiter passes 190 requests in 60 seconds against a limit of 100 requests a minute. A client can bypass a fixed-window limiter simply by timing its bursts to the minute boundary. More accurate algorithms trade memory for precision.

A **sliding log** records the timestamp of every allowed request in the last minute and refuses new requests when the log already holds 100 timestamps. It is exact, and expensive: at 100 requests a second over a 60-second window, a key's log holds 6,000 timestamps of 8 bytes each (48 KB), so a million busy keys would require 48 GB of RAM. A **sliding window counter** keeps only the current minute's count and the previous minute's count. It estimates the last 60 seconds of traffic by weighting the previous minute's count by the overlapping time: 15 seconds into the current minute, it sums 75% of the previous minute's count and 100% of the current minute's count. This takes only two integers per key and closely approximates the sliding log. You can compare the number of requests each algorithm allows in the figure's readout.

A **token bucket** reverses the accounting. Each key has a bucket that refills with tokens at the allowed rate (100 tokens a minute here) up to a fixed capacity; each request takes one token, and the limiter refuses any request that finds the bucket empty. The refill rate sets the sustained average rate, while the bucket capacity sets the maximum burst a client may send after an idle period. Over any span of *T* seconds, a bucket of capacity *b* tokens refilling at *r* tokens a second passes at most *b* + *rT* requests. A bucket whose capacity equals a whole minute's allowance can therefore pass twice the per-minute limit across a minute, just as the fixed window did; select Token bucket in the figure and adjust the Bucket size slider to see this behaviour. The bucket's state requires two numbers (the remaining tokens and the timestamp of the last refill), and the limiter calculates the refill lazily when the next request arrives, so no background timer runs between requests.[^leaky]

blocks.title: What each costs a key
points: Fixed window: one counter; can pass twice the limit across a boundary.
Sliding log: one timestamp per request in the window; exact, but kilobytes per busy key.
Sliding window counter: two counters; approximate, close enough.
Token bucket: two numbers; a sustained rate plus a burst you choose.

blocks.text: The API runs on many gateway machines behind a load balancer, and a key's requests land on whichever gateway the balancer picks. If each gateway kept its own independent count, a client would get its full rate limit multiplied by the number of gateways. You must either share the count across gateways or split the limit among them. We can calculate whether sharing the count in a central store is affordable.

**An estimate.** We can store each key's token bucket as a small hash in Redis, the in-memory store from lesson 14. The key's name, two numbers and Redis's internal metadata take about 100 bytes, so a million keys require about 100 MB of RAM, which fits easily in a single machine's memory. Every API request requires one call to Redis, so 50,000 requests a second generate 50,000 Redis calls a second. One single-threaded Redis process handles roughly 100,000 simple operations a second on one CPU core, so three Redis processes, each holding a third of the keys by hash and backed by a replica, can serve the peak load with spare capacity. A network round trip inside a datacentre takes a few hundred microseconds (lesson 1), which fits within our 1 ms latency budget.

Sharing a counter creates a race condition. If two gateways handle requests for the same key at the same instant, both read *tokens = 1*, both allow the request, and both write *tokens = 0*, letting two requests pass on one token. During a traffic flood, that race occurs thousands of times a second. Before reading on, consider how you would prevent it without holding a distributed lock across the network. In practice, engineers send the entire check-and-decrement logic to Redis as a single script. Redis executes the script from start to finish before running any other command, making the read, the decision and the write **atomic**, so no other command can interleave between them.[^lua] The diagram below shows the stored fields and the script logic.

blocks.caption: A token bucket as Redis holds it, the script that spends a token, and what a refused client receives.

blocks.text: The alternative is to split the limit: give each of the *n* gateways its own local bucket at 1/*n* of the total rate, avoiding network calls to a shared store. This approach is cheap and accurate on average, but it fails in two cases. First, if a client sends all its requests over a single long-lived connection pinned to one gateway, it receives only a quarter of its limit when there are four gateways. Second, adding a fifth gateway changes every gateway's share unless you reconfigure all of them. A middle ground is to keep the authoritative count in Redis while gateways lease tokens in batches: a gateway fetches 20 tokens for a key at once and spends them locally, reducing Redis traffic by a factor of 20. The trade-off is that a client can exceed its limit by up to 20 tokens per gateway holding a batch, or up to 40 extra requests across the two gateways in our figure.

Engineers place the limiter in the API gateway, after authentication, because the limiter needs the API key and the route, which are only available once the gateway has parsed the HTTP request.[^l4l7] Adding a second limiter inside an individual backend service lets you enforce service-specific rules (such as allowing only one concurrent export job per customer). Putting the limiter only in client libraries protects nothing, because a buggy client is the very one that will bypass it.

In the workbench below, two tenants share an API that can serve 200 requests a second across eight worker threads, with each request taking 40 ms of processing time. Tenant B sends a steady 40 requests a second. You can set Tenant A's request rate and choose the limiter configuration: no limiter, a local bucket in each gateway, or shared buckets in Redis, with each tenant limited to 80 requests a second. The simulation runs in slow motion with stretched network delays so you can follow individual requests; the reported latencies are in simulation milliseconds rather than real-world network times. To test a Redis outage, select shared buckets in Redis, set *If Redis is down* to fail open or fail closed, and click the Redis node to take it offline.

blocks.caption: Two tenants, a balancer, two gateways and an API with room for about 200 requests a second. Blue dots are requests, green answers, red failures; amber shows how busy a part is.
blocks.task: Turn tenant A up to 300 requests a second or more with a limiter on

blocks.text: With no limiter, setting Tenant A to 400 requests a second fills the API's request queue, forcing Tenant B's requests to wait behind Tenant A's. Once the queue is full, the API drops incoming requests, causing more than half of Tenant B's traffic to fail through no fault of Tenant B. With either limiter enabled, Tenant A gets 80 requests a second allowed and about 320 requests a second refused. The gateway answers each refusal in 0.5 ms instead of the API spending 40 ms, so Tenant B's traffic is unaffected. Refusing a request must take far less compute time than serving it, or the refusals themselves will overload the system.

**Handling a Redis failure.** When Redis crashes, every gateway queries a store that does not respond. If the gateway treats a failed query as a refusal, it **fails closed**, and the API rejects every request from every tenant. The limiter, built to protect the API, has caused a total outage. If the gateway treats a failed query as permission to proceed, it **fails open**, and no requests are rate-limited until Redis recovers, which matches normal operation on most days anyway. For a limiter guarding against occasional traffic floods, you should fail open, set a 1 ms to 2 ms timeout on the Redis call so a degraded Redis instance does not add latency to every request, and page an engineer to fix the store. A limiter that prevents brute-force password guessing has the opposite security requirement and should fail closed. Test both behaviours using the *If Redis is down* setting in the workbench.

A refusal response should also tell the client when to retry. Returning an HTTP 429 status code with a Retry-After header tells the client how long to wait;[^status] a well-behaved client waits for that duration plus random jitter so its retries do not synchronise with other clients (lesson 18). A client that retries immediately turns one refused request into a continuous flood, which is why gateways count all incoming attempts against the rate limit rather than only successful requests.

**Choosing the numbers.** Engineers typically set a token bucket's capacity to a few seconds' worth of its refill rate. A key allowed 100 requests a second gets a bucket capacity of 200 to 500 tokens, which accommodates a web page firing a burst of API calls as it loads, while clamping a runaway loop down to the sustained rate within a few seconds. You can size a concurrency cap using Little's law (lesson 2): the average number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average response time. At 100 requests a second and a normal latency of 50 ms (0.05 seconds), a client has 5 requests in flight on average; setting a cap at four or five times that normal level (20 to 25 concurrent requests) leaves headroom for minor latency spikes while stopping a client from exhausting worker threads if an endpoint slows tenfold. Set the timeout on the Redis call just above Redis's 99th-percentile latency, around 1 ms inside a datacentre, so a healthy Redis instance rarely trips it. Finally, set a load shedder's reserved capacity to match the critical traffic's share of the peak hour: if payment charges represent 20% of peak traffic, reserve 20% of fleet capacity for them.
Tarjan's post described four limiters at Stripe: two that restrict individual users and two that shed load to protect the fleet as a whole.

**A request rate limiter**: a token bucket per user stored in Redis, matching the design we built above. This limiter refused far more requests than the other three, and Tarjan noted that a large fraction of the rejected requests were test-mode traffic from customer scripts that had gone haywire. **A concurrent requests limiter**: a cap on how many requests a single user may have in flight at the same time, such as 20 concurrent requests. A per-second rate limit fails to protect the fleet when backend requests get slower. By Little's law (lesson 2), the number of requests in flight equals the request rate multiplied by the response time. If a user sends 10 requests a second to an endpoint whose latency degrades from 100 ms to 10 seconds, the user's in-flight requests climb from 1 to 100, occupying 100 worker threads without ever exceeding a 10-requests-per-second rate limit.

**A fleet usage load shedder**: Stripe divided its API calls into critical requests (such as creating a charge) and non-critical requests, reserving a fraction of total fleet capacity for the critical ones. In the post's example, reserving 20% of capacity for critical calls means that non-critical requests are rejected with an HTTP 503 status code once total fleet utilisation exceeds 80%. **A worker utilisation load shedder**: this acts as the last line of defence on each individual server. When a server's worker threads are nearly full, it sheds incoming traffic in four priority tiers: test-mode traffic first, then live GET requests, then non-critical live POSTs, and critical methods last. As worker utilisation drops, the shedder restores traffic gradually so the server does not oscillate between overload and idle.

Stripe's per-key rate limiter matches the design from the first half of this lesson, while its load shedders solve a problem our initial exercise did not address. Per-key limits check whether a single client is sending too much traffic, but they do not help when every client stays under its individual limit and the combined traffic still exceeds what the fleet can handle, such as during a flash sale or when a third of the backend servers are down. Priority load shedding handles fleet-wide overload. Tarjan also recommended launching every new limiter in dark mode, logging the requests it would have refused before enforcing rejections in production, and maintaining a feature flag to disable the limiter immediately if needed.[^dark]

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **At 500,000 requests a second**, the Redis cluster scales to a dozen or so shards, each owning a slice of keys by hash, and the bottleneck shifts from total cluster throughput to the single busiest key. A single tenant sending 50,000 requests a second routes all of those checks to the one Redis shard that owns its key, consuming half of that shard's capacity on a single bucket. Leasing tokens in batches solves this hot-key bottleneck: if each gateway checks out 100 tokens per Redis call, it reduces Redis operations for that key by a factor of 100, while bounding the maximum overshoot to 100 tokens multiplied by the number of gateways.

**At 5 million requests a second across three geographic regions**, a single key's requests may arrive at datacentres on different continents, where cross-region network round trips take 70 ms to 150 ms. Querying a single global token bucket on every request would blow the latency budget. Instead, engineers allocate each region a local share of each key's limit. Every few seconds, the regions report each key's actual consumption and rebalance the regional shares toward where the traffic is arriving. If a client's traffic shifts abruptly from one region to another, the client can exceed its global limit for a few seconds by the unused allowance left in the old region, well beyond our 10% accuracy target. We relax the accuracy requirement here because the backend can tolerate a few seconds of overshoot, whereas it cannot tolerate 100 ms of cross-continental latency on every request. At this scale, engineers distribute the table of rate limits as configuration pushed directly to every gateway's memory, rolling it out with the same staged deployment safeguards as any other fleet-wide configuration change (lesson D7).

blocks.caption: Seven questions on limiters
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A limit of 100 requests a minute is counted in fixed windows that reset on the minute. How can a client get nearly 200 requests through in one 60-second span?
choices: By sending about 100 requests just before a minute ends and 100 requests just after, so each window sees under its limit
By opening two connections, because each connection is counted against its own separate window
By sending its requests faster than the counter can be written, so some are never counted at all
items.why: Each window only counts its own requests. Two bursts on either side of a boundary land in different windows, so both pass within a few seconds of each other.

items.ask: A token bucket refills at 10 tokens a second and holds at most 50 tokens. What is the most a client can send in any 10-second span?
choices: 100 requests: the refill rate times the span, whatever the bucket holds when the span begins
150 requests: a full bucket of 50 tokens spent at once, plus 100 tokens of refill over 10 seconds
50 requests: the bucket's maximum size
items.why: A burst can spend the 50 tokens already in the bucket, and the refill adds 10 tokens a second over the 10-second span: b + rT = 50 + (10 × 10) = 150 requests.

items.ask: Two gateways share a token bucket in Redis, and each runs GET, decides, then SET as separate commands. What goes wrong under a flood?
choices: Redis runs out of memory, because every GET and SET pair leaves an extra copy of the bucket behind it
Both gateways read the same last token, both spend it, and more requests pass than the limit allows
The SET from one gateway is refused, so the other gateway's requests all fail until the key expires
items.why: Separate read and write steps leave a gap in which another gateway can read the same value. A script that Redis runs atomically closes the gap.

items.ask: A per-key limiter guards an API against occasional floods; its Redis store fails. Which response is usually best, and why?
choices: Fail closed and refuse all requests, since an unlimited API can't be trusted to stay up through a flood
Retry Redis until it answers
Fail open with a short timeout, since a rare flood costs less than a total API outage
items.why: Failing closed turns a Redis failure into a total API outage, while unlimited traffic for a short period matches normal operation on most days. A login limiter is the exception.

items.ask: A customer sends a steady 10 requests a second, well within its rate limit, but the endpoint it calls slows from 100 ms to 10 s per request. What protects the servers?
choices: A tighter rate limit, since 10 requests a second is now too many for an endpoint that slow to answer
A concurrency limit, which notices that requests in flight have risen from about 1 to about 100
A longer timeout, so each slow request has time to finish and free its thread
items.why: By Little's law, the number of requests in flight rises from about 1 to about 100 while the arrival rate stays the same; only a cap on concurrent requests in progress catches this.

items.ask: Each of 4 gateways keeps its own token bucket at a quarter of a key's 100-requests-a-second limit. A client holds one long-lived connection, pinned to one gateway. What rate does it get?
choices: About 25 requests a second, one gateway's quarter share
About 100 requests a second, the sum of the four buckets
About 400 requests a second, because each gateway grants the full limit to whatever traffic it sees
items.why: Splitting a limit across gateways assumes traffic spreads evenly across all four machines. A pinned client reaches only one gateway's bucket.

items.ask: A fleet is at 120% of capacity. Most customers send far below their rate limits, and none is over. Which design keeps payments working?
choices: Lower every customer's rate limit by 20% until the fleet is back under its capacity
Shed load by priority, reserving capacity for payment charges
Queue every request until capacity frees up
items.why: Customers sending far below their rate limits are unaffected when you lower those limits, and queueing requests only increases latency during sustained overload. Refusing lower-priority work first while reserving capacity for payment charges is how Stripe's fleet-wide load shedders keep payments running.

summary: **Pin down what the limiter is for.** Enforcing per-key limits, returning clear refusal headers and shedding load by priority belong in the limiter; stopping packet floods, billing customers and revoking stolen keys belong elsewhere.
**Fixed windows leak at the boundary.** Two bursts on either side of a window reset can pass nearly twice the limit in a 60-second span.
**A token bucket enforces a sustained rate plus a burst.** It stores two numbers per key, refills lazily, and passes at most b + rT requests over any span T.
**A sliding log is exact and costly; a sliding counter is cheap and close.** Accuracy within a few per cent is sufficient for rate limiting.
**Shared counts need one atomic step.** Read, decide and write inside a single Redis Lua script, or concurrent gateways will spend the same token twice.
**Decide how the limiter fails.** Fail open for general flood protection, fail closed for login rate limiting, and always enforce a short timeout on the store.
**Refusing must be far cheaper than serving.** Returning HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header at the gateway takes microseconds, while client backoff and jitter prevent retry storms.
**Rate limits miss slow requests; concurrency limits catch them.** By Little's law, a slower endpoint holds more requests in flight at the same arrival rate.
**Per-key limits can't save an overloaded fleet.** Stripe reserved capacity for critical requests and shed test traffic and read requests first.
**At scale, batch and split.** Lease tokens in batches to handle hot keys, and allocate each geographic region a local share of a global limit.

leaky.title: The leaky bucket
leaky.text: A **leaky bucket** is the token bucket's counterpart: incoming requests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rate, and the limiter refuses any request that finds the queue full. Whereas a token bucket allows a burst to pass immediately up to the bucket capacity, a leaky bucket smooths bursts into an even output stream, which suits a sender feeding a slow downstream service but requires maintaining a queue per key. Telecommunications engineers used both algorithms in the 1980s and 1990s to police and shape traffic on telephone and ATM networks.

lua.title: Atomic scripts in Redis
lua.text: Redis executes commands sequentially on a single thread, so a Lua script sent with EVAL runs from start to finish with no other command interleaved. That makes reading the bucket, checking the count and writing the new state a single atomic step without distributed locks. Because a slow script blocks every other client connected to that Redis process, engineers keep rate-limiter scripts down to a few arithmetic operations.

l4l7.title: Layer 4 and layer 7
l4l7.text: A **layer 4** load balancer inspects only TCP connections, IP addresses and ports; it is fast and simple but cannot read the HTTP request inside a connection. A **layer 7** load balancer or API gateway terminates TLS and parses HTTP, so it can route by URL path, verify credentials and enforce a rate limit per API key. Most architectures use both: a layer 4 balancer distributes TCP connections across a pool of layer 7 gateways, which perform the per-request inspection. Gateways also drain connections before a restart, finishing in-flight requests before closing the socket.

status.title: 429 and 503
status.text: HTTP status 429 (Too Many Requests), defined in RFC 6585 in 2012, tells a client that it has exceeded its rate limit. Status 503 (Service Unavailable) indicates that the server is overloaded regardless of the individual client's rate, making it the appropriate status code for a load shedder. Both responses can include a Retry-After header specifying a wait time in seconds or an HTTP timestamp.

dark.title: Launching a limiter in the dark
dark.text: When you deploy a new rate limiter, its initial thresholds are estimates until you test them against production traffic. Running the limiter in dark mode, where it logs requests that exceed the threshold without actually rejecting them, shows which legitimate customers would be affected and lets you tune the limits from real traffic data before returning a single HTTP 429 response.
